Triggers.value: A memory of the event coming to mind suddenly

Threat.value: I jump or startle at ordinary sounds that would not bother most people
Suddenly feeling or acting as if the stressful experience were actually happening again
I am unable to relax even when I know I am in a safe place

Memory.value: The memory feels like it belongs to someone else rather than to me
My memories of the event feel more real and vivid than memories of ordinary things
Remembering what happened during the frightening event is just like looking at photographs of it in my mind.

Negative Appraisals.value: I feel like I don't know myself anymore
I can't deal with even the slightest upset
The event happened because of the way I acted

vignette: The kidnapping occurred during a routine residential call two years ago when a compromised floor gave way and she was taken by a group that had been using the basement as a holding cell. For forty-three days, Clara Vance was stripped of her agency, bound in the dark, and forced to endure a suffocating silence that shattered her sense of self. Returning to the firehouse felt less like a homecoming and more like stepping into a different life. The station's breakroom, once a place of dry humor, now housed a wall of commemorative photos that acted as immediate catalysts. Each framed smile from past drills and promotions triggered a sudden, chilling recall, pulling the darkness of the basement directly into her mind. The more she stared at those images, the more certain she became that her survival was a mistake, directly tied to her own hesitation on that job. She had come to believe she didn't know herself anymore, that the woman who had survived was a stranger who had failed to protect her own skin. This erosion of self-worth quickly poisoned her perception of safety. Believing she was fundamentally broken and incapable of handling even minor stress, Clara found herself constantly braced for disaster. Her body never stopped sounding the alarm; ordinary clatters of a coffee mug or the sudden slam of a bay door sent her jumping, her pulse hammering against her ribs. This relentless tension made it impossible to unwind, even in her own apartment where she knew she was secure. The inability to relax only deepened her conviction that she had lost her coping ability. Her persistent self-doubt actively distorted her recall, making the memories feel more real and vivid than normal, while her conviction that she couldn't cope pushed her away from crowded emergency scenes. When the memory felt just like looking at photographs in her mind, it suddenly made her feel as though the stressful experience were actually happening again. The photographic clarity of the event then flooded her with self-reproach, convincing her that the captivity had happened because of the way she acted. These vivid intrusions made her hyper-aware of old photos and the crush of public spaces, which in turn made her scan the station corridors for familiar threats. Her constant startle and inability to relax even when safe only deepened how real and vivid the memories felt, making them feel like they belonged to someone else rather than to her. Her hypervigilance made ordinary crowds and old photographs feel inescapable, while the relentless tension reinforced her belief that she couldn't deal with even the slightest upset and had permanently lost herself. At work, the loop manifested in quiet but irreversible shifts. During a routine high-rise call, a sudden crowd of onlookers and flashing lights triggered a startle response so severe she doubled over, mistaking the scene for the basement. Her captain had to pull her back, and Clara immediately interpreted her collapse as proof of her broken coping capacity. She stopped volunteering for complex searches, choosing instead to stick to equipment checks in the quietest corners of the station. The detachment from her crew grew palpable; she could no longer sit through debriefs without her mind drifting back to the alien, detached feeling of the memories. The weight of carrying this unspoken fracture finally broke her resolve during a department wellness review. Standing in the administrative office, staring at a mandatory counseling referral, Clara realized she was more afraid of her own reactions than the fire itself. She signed the form not because she expected a cure, but because she was desperate to understand why her own mind had turned into a prison, and she hoped, for the first time in months, that someone might finally help her find the exit.
